newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Unease grips Albania over failed pyramid schemes.
newsitem.headline: Unease grips Albania over failed pyramid schemes.

text.p: Unease gripped Albanians on Saturday awaiting action on the government's promise to refund some of the money millions of impoverished depositors ploughed into failed pyramid schemes.
Central Tirana, where protesters demanding the return of their savings clashed with police last weekend, bustled instead with curbside hawkers offering a wide range of household goods.

Albania's opposition, emboldened by newfound unity, planned protests on Sunday in the capital and two other cities against rightist President Sali Berisha and his government. The biggest group, the Socialists, accused authorities of intimidation.
The official ATA news agency said government supporters had staged rallies of their own in the Balkan country to denounce the violence of the past three weeks. It gave no details.

Berisha has pledged that the government will do its best to give back whatever money it can from funds frozen by banks. Most is made up of funds sent home by Albanians working abroad since the 1990 fall of a hardline communist regime.
The poorest depositors would be given cash, he said, while others would receive government certificates or shares, an offer already angrily dismissed by many savers.
"I've invested $1,500 for medical treatment abroad. That's half the money my son sent to me from Italy," said a 69-year-old widow in her neat but crumbling one-room apartment.
"Berisha is our only hope. I have nothing against him or the government. All I ask is my money back just to survive."
Reduced to living on a monthly pension equivalent to $40, the widow was too afraid to give her name -- like nearly everyone questioned in the capital.
At least 149 people have been detained after three weeks of unrest in which government buildings and offices of Berisha's ruling Democratic Party have been set on fire.
The Interior Ministry has said prosecutors will be seeking 15-year jail terms for those accused of instigating violence.
Leading Socialist Ndre Legisi, his head heavily bandaged, told reporters from his hospital bed he had been attacked by unknown assailants in central Tirana in the presence of police.
"I was beaten in Fortuzi street," Legisi said. "The street is the best lit and most heavily controlled by secret police in Tirana because the president used to live there."

Eyewitness accounts say police were checking border posts and hotels near them to ensure suspects do not escape their dragnet in Europe's poorest country, once isolated from the rest of the world under communist dictator Enver Hoxha.

Opposition parties, which this week formed a new group, the Forum for Democracy, planned Sunday rallies in the Adriatic port of Durres and in Lezhe, further north. Trade unionists led by Azem Hajdari, who helped organise anti-communist student protests in 1990, were to gather on Tirana soccer pitch.
Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million has put some money into the schemes, lured by high regular interest payments. But the schemes began to crumble a few months ago.
Tirana newspapers have reported at least two suicides by ruined depositors. A third was said to have lost his mind.
The crisis has sent the lek currency into a nosedive. It has lost 30 percent against the dollar since the New Year.
The Socialists and Berisha's Democrats have accused each other of using proceeds from pyramid schemes to fund last May's general election campaign.
The Democrats won the election and have a stranglehold on parliament, boycotted by the opposition. Western observers say the election was plagued by serious irregularities.
